title: Gibraltar's New EU Deal: Trade, Sovereignty and the Border
label: 15 September 2026 · UK-EU Gibraltar agreement
summary: The European Affairs Committee questioned Lord Wood of Anfield and Paul Hughes about the new UK-EU treaty on Gibraltar. The deal aims to keep the Gibraltar-Spain land border fluid by aligning Gibraltar with certain EU rules, while the UK insists sovereignty is untouched. The hearing explored how it works in practice, why it took five years, and lingering concerns about Spain's role, military access, and exit clauses.

speakers.label: Lord Wood of Anfield
speakers.name: Lord Wood of Anfield
speakers.role: Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State, Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO)

speakers.label: Paul Hughes
speakers.name: Paul Hughes
speakers.role: Deputy Head of the Southern Europe Department, Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO)

chapters.title: Why a bespoke deal was needed
chapters.takeaway: Gibraltar was left out of the 2020 trade deal, so the UK, Gibraltar, Spain and the EU negotiated a separate treaty to keep the border fluid.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Welcome, Minister. Why wasn't Gibraltar included in the 2020 trade and cooperation agreement in the first place? And why did it take five years to get this new deal?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: Good morning, Chair. Gibraltar wasn't in the TCA mainly because the EU—and Spain in particular—wanted separate arrangements. Gibraltar's needs are different, so the previous government agreed to pursue a bespoke deal instead.

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: The goal was always a fluid border between Gibraltar and Spain. Without a deal, disruption could have cost hundreds of millions and threatened jobs and investment. The bridging measures helped for a while but were informal and couldn't last, especially with the EU's new entry/exit system coming in.

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: As for the five years: it's a hugely complex treaty—over a thousand pages, covering customs, airports, military issues, and more. And politics got in the way: UK political turmoil in 2022, Spanish elections in 2023, and a change of government here in 2024. Talks continued but the pace slowed.

chapters.title: What a fluid border really means
chapters.takeaway: The deal lets the 15,000 people who cross the land border daily do so without checks, which is vital for Gibraltar's economy.

turns.speaker: Lord Jackson of Peterborough
turns.text: You talk about 'fluidity at the frontier'. What does that actually mean in practice? Is it the same as free movement?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: Not the same. Fluidity means the 15,000 people who cross the land border every day can pass without checks. That's the key to Gibraltar's economy. Air and sea arrivals have different arrangements. The people of Gibraltar made clear this was the most important thing.

chapters.title: How the deal is governed
chapters.takeaway: A complex web of joint committees and diplomatic resources will oversee the treaty, but no big increase in UK resources is expected.

turns.speaker: Lord Grantchester
turns.text: The agreement creates a lot of new structures—cooperation councils, committees, dispute resolution. How will the UK navigate all that? Will you need extra diplomats?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: You're right that it's complex. There's a ministerial-led cooperation council, three specialised committees, and dispute resolution mechanisms—similar to the withdrawal agreement. We also have the Gibraltar team in the FCDO, the Governor's team in Gibraltar, our mission in Brussels, and our embassy in Madrid all engaging.

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: I visited Gibraltar last week for National Day—I even wore red trousers and a red tie! The Governor and his team do excellent work. We don't expect this to require a significant increase in resources.

chapters.title: Sovereignty: red lines and real choices
chapters.takeaway: The UK insists the treaty doesn't touch sovereignty, but Lord Moynihan challenges whether aligning Gibraltar with EU customs rules impinges on British trade policy.

turns.speaker: Baroness Ashton of Upholland
turns.text: Minister, there were principles set out in 2021 about what should and shouldn't be done on sovereignty. Did you have to bump up against any of those? Do you feel comfortable that sovereignty is fully protected?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: Categorically, this treaty doesn't affect sovereignty at all. Article 2 explicitly says the treaty can't be used to challenge the sovereignty position. Sovereignty wasn't discussed. The arrangements are bespoke to Gibraltar's unique circumstances and were chosen by the Government of Gibraltar and supported unanimously by its parliament.

turns.speaker: Lord Moynihan of Chelsea
turns.text: But surely this removes Gibraltar from British trade policy permanently? Would Gibraltar still be allowed to join the CPTPP?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: It doesn't touch sovereignty. The customs arrangements were Gibraltar's choice. Paul, can you answer on CPTPP?

turns.speaker: Paul Hughes
turns.text: The treaty is only about goods trade. Gibraltar has established a customs union with the EU for goods. It could accede to CPTPP for services—just not goods, because of that customs union.

turns.speaker: Lord Moynihan of Chelsea
turns.text: That's my point. We have a policy of not joining the EU customs union, but now Gibraltar is in one for goods. That impinges on our trade policy.

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: Lord Moynihan, I don't think that's true. Gibraltar isn't joining the EU customs union. It has a bespoke customs union for goods with the EU—that's different. It's a choice they made.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: On sovereignty, some might worry about a creeping expansion of Spain's role—Spanish customs, police, etc. How is that controlled?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: There are clearly delineated limits. For example, Spanish military officers are only involved in military derogations and limited information sharing. They have no jurisdictional role. More cooperation is what makes the treaty work, but it's carefully scoped.

chapters.title: Dispute resolution and the ECJ
chapters.takeaway: The arbitration mechanism borrows from the withdrawal agreement, with a limited role for the European Court of Justice.

turns.speaker: Lord Tugendhat
turns.text: I'm intrigued by the dispute arbitration procedure. Could it be a precedent for the UK's current negotiations with the EU on things like electricity and carbon emissions?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: I'm not an expert on the details, but there are parallels—like aligning on regulations. Paul, can you say more about the dispute mechanism?

turns.speaker: Paul Hughes
turns.text: It's largely standard, except for how it deals with EU law—there's a potential referral to the ECJ. That mechanism was taken from the withdrawal agreement and previous EU agreements. It could serve as a basis for other negotiations.

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: To be clear, the ECJ's role is just clarifying aspects of EU law for the parts Gibraltar has taken on board.

chapters.title: Military base and Schengen checks
chapters.takeaway: The treaty protects UK military autonomy in Gibraltar, with no Spanish role in operations, and special arrangements for military personnel crossing borders.

turns.speaker: The Duke of Wellington
turns.text: I declare my historic interests in Spain. Will this treaty affect military personnel coming and going, and the general access to the naval and military base?

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: And could you address the conduct of operations as well?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: Safeguarding the operational autonomy of UK military facilities was a total red line. There's no Spanish role in approving or controlling our operations or deployments. Military personnel, defence civilians, and their families won't be subject to routine Schengen checks.

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: We do have limited information sharing with Spanish military liaison officers—they're a NATO ally—but only to facilitate military derogations. The Commander British Forces is very positive about the early cooperation.

turns.speaker: The Duke of Wellington
turns.text: So local commanders are content? Perhaps they even see it as an improvement?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: Absolutely. I was struck by the positivity. It's only been two months, but relationship-building is going well.

turns.speaker: Baroness Smith of Newnham
turns.text: I visited Gibraltar last year. You said service personnel won't be subject to routine Schengen checks. Will they have a document so they don't get caught by the 90-days-in-180 rule when visiting other Schengen countries?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: Yes. They need a standard document like a valid ID or movement order. And there's now an arrangement for military personnel to 'clock in and out' so the Schengen clock stops and starts correctly. That's an implementation improvement from the last couple of months.

chapters.title: Who decides who enters Gibraltar?
chapters.takeaway: Gibraltar keeps control of entry, but has agreed to mutually recognise Spanish refusals into Schengen based on security concerns.

turns.speaker: Lord Brennan of Canton
turns.text: How will refusal of individual entry work? Who takes the final decision to exclude someone, and when?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: Gibraltar has controlled entry for decades and still does. Gibraltar residents can't be refused entry—they have the right to return home. At the airport, everyone goes through Gibraltar immigration first, then Spanish Schengen checks. If Spain refuses entry into Schengen on security grounds, Gibraltar has chosen to mutually recognise that decision.

turns.speaker: Lord Brennan of Canton
turns.text: So Spanish authorities could effectively refuse entry into Gibraltar?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: No—Spain decides on Schengen entry. Gibraltar takes that information and makes its own decision, but they've chosen mutual recognition as the principle.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What about the reverse? If Spain wants to allow someone in but Gibraltar doesn't?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: Gibraltar has the right to exclude anyone from Gibraltar, including UK nationals who aren't residents. They're in charge of admission to Gibraltar.

turns.speaker: Paul Hughes
turns.text: Everyone goes through both sets of checks. Gibraltar could say 'you're not coming into Gibraltar' even if Spain admits them into Schengen.

turns.speaker: Lord Brennan of Canton
turns.text: What about non-EU citizens? Would the same apply?

turns.speaker: Paul Hughes
turns.text: I'd have to check and come back to you. I think the principle of transit home applies, but I'm not certain.

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: We'll definitely clarify that point.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Yes, please do. I was baffled by that part too. And the Chief Minister is coming later, so he might help.

turns.speaker: Lord Brennan of Canton
turns.text: One more thing, Minister: has anyone asked President Trump his opinion on Gibraltar, given he's opined on the Falklands and Northern Ireland?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: I haven't done a trawl of his social media recently, so I don't know. I don't believe he has, but I can't be sure.

chapters.title: Annexes, alignment and jobs
chapters.takeaway: The UK rejects claims that 43 annexes of EU law diminish sovereignty, saying only about eight contain EU law and they were Gibraltar's choice.

turns.speaker: Lord Jackson of Peterborough
turns.text: The treaty contains 43 annexes of EU legal acquis applying to Gibraltar dynamically. In 2024, the Commons EU committee warned of a 'serious diminution of UK sovereignty'. Spain gets powers over arrest, residency permits, and even banning residents from leaving. Is Article 2 enough to address that?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: Sovereignty hasn't been diminished. These are areas where Gibraltar is choosing to align to unlock benefits. And it's not true that there are 43 annexes of EU law—most are procedural or lists. Only about eight contain EU law. It's a bespoke deal, proportionate to Gibraltar's circumstances, and they decided to do it.

turns.speaker: Lord Jackson of Peterborough
turns.text: With respect, that's separate. We're talking about the sovereignty of a British territory, regardless of whether Gibraltar agrees.

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: We have a consistent principle: 'Nothing about Gibraltar without Gibraltar'. The people of Gibraltar made these choices and we respect them. This model avoids imposing irrelevant EU law and supports their economy.

turns.speaker: Lord Jackson of Peterborough
turns.text: Finally, there's concern that the treaty gives the EU and Spain power to de facto block British nationals from working in Spain, displacing employment opportunities. Is that a fair concern?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: I don't recognise that description. Gibraltar remains in charge of who comes in. Yes, there are economic changes, but the treaty provides legal certainty, which Gibraltarians have welcomed.

chapters.title: Money, concordat and termination
chapters.takeaway: A political concordat clarifies UK-Gibraltar cooperation, while termination clauses allow exit in specific scenarios—including a possible Spanish-triggered review after four years.

turns.speaker: Lord Elliott of Mickle Fell
turns.text: The agreement mentions a financial mechanism for regional cohesion. How much will Gibraltar pay, and will the UK contribute?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: Both parties will set up independent funds. Gibraltar's fund could support training for frontier workers. No specific timelines yet. And under the concordat, the UK contribution comes from Gibraltar, not UK taxpayers.

turns.speaker: Lord Barrow
turns.text: I declare my interest in having worked on related agreements. Why was the concordat necessary, and what's its impact?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: It's a political agreement between the UK and Gibraltar to clarify how we work together on implementation. It sets out responsibilities while respecting constitutional arrangements. Similar to one under the withdrawal agreement. It's essential for smooth operation.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What's the legal status of the concordat versus the treaty?

turns.speaker: Paul Hughes
turns.text: It's a political instrument between us and the Government of Gibraltar. No legal standing.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: So it's open to amendment by either side—driven by political considerations?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: Whoever is in government, we have a vested interest in a working relationship with Gibraltar. They need clarity. I'm hopeful it continues.

turns.speaker: Lord Moynihan of Chelsea
turns.text: On termination, Article 334 requires 12 months' notice and a referendum, but Article 19.5 allows termination in 90 days, and Spain can unilaterally force termination. Have I got that right?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: Article 19.5 is precedented in EU agreements with Norway, Switzerland and Iceland. It's for a specific scenario where Gibraltar rejects an EU Act update. There's a 90-day discussion period to avoid it kicking in. As for Spain, Paul knows more.

turns.speaker: Paul Hughes
turns.text: The article you mean is in the mobility chapter, after a four-year review. If Spain informs the EU it's no longer content, the EU can start termination. It reflects that most of the treaty affects Spain. It's not 'at any time'—it's a specific process at that review.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: So the Spanish option is a one-off at that four-year point? Can you confirm and come back to us?

turns.speaker: Paul Hughes
turns.text: I'm fairly certain, yes. The Chief Minister will be able to say for sure.

chapters.title: Wrapping up: a lasting settlement?
chapters.takeaway: The minister sees the treaty as the final piece of the Brexit jigsaw, with implementation now the focus.

turns.speaker: Lord Tugendhat
turns.text: It feels like negotiations on Gibraltar have been going on forever. Do you think this agreement settles matters for the foreseeable future, or will more be needed?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: From a treaty point of view, yes—it's the last piece of the Brexit jigsaw. Sovereignty is protected completely. There will be implementation adjustments, but this is a stable and lasting foundation for Gibraltar's relationship with the EU.

turns.speaker: Lord Tugendhat
turns.text: That's very encouraging. Congratulations to all involved.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you, Minister and Mr Hughes, for your evidence. It's been a pleasure. We're on time, so we'll conclude here.
